strengths: The motivation is useful: increasing agent count can make exploration easier, so a predefined few-to-more curriculum can be inappropriate. Adaptively selecting agent counts is a reasonable contribution to sparse-reward MARL.
SPMARL is a simple modification of SPRL that reuses the underlying critic loss. The direct comparison with SPRL helps assess the incremental contribution of this objective.

Experiments cover three qualitatively different cooperative settings and evaluate performance on fixed target tasks. Simple-Spread and SMACv2 show promising early learning improvements. Curriculum trajectories aid interpretation, and Simple-Spread explicitly reports five seeds with 95% confidence intervals.
The manuscript provides pseudocode, discusses practical handling of variable agent counts, and supplies a code link.
weaknesses: The central interpretation of critic loss as learning progress is inadequately justified. In Equation 8, expected squared return-prediction error contains both value-approximation error and conditional return variance. Even an accurate critic for a fixed policy can therefore have substantial loss without useful policy improvement. Access to the full state does not eliminate this problem. No direct measurements establish that the proposed score tracks subsequent policy improvement or alleviates credit assignment, leaving the principal mechanistic claims unsupported.

The curriculum optimization is not mathematically well defined as written. Equation 6 minimizes KL(p || μ) while describing μ as a Dirac distribution; this divergence is infinite whenever the curriculum assigns probability outside the target. An implementable target approximation or alternative objective must be specified. There is also a procedural inconsistency: Algorithm 1 returns to first-stage optimization whenever performance falls below the threshold, whereas Section 4.1 describes freezing the distribution after entering the second stage.

The baseline suite does not substantiate the broad comparison with existing multi-agent curriculum methods. FewToMore, EPC, and VACL are replaced by a linear schedule, omitting their other mechanisms. In Simple-Spread, that schedule increases agent count despite the paper's own explanation that fewer agents make exploration harder. A suitably tuned decreasing schedule and stronger automatic curriculum baselines would make the comparison more convincing.

The originality of critic-error-based task selection is insufficiently situated. Related approaches such as Prioritized Level Replay already use value-error-based scores to prioritize training environments. Comparisons with such methods and with reward-improvement-based learning-progress curricula are missing. The adaptation to agent-count curricula may be useful, but the manuscript does not clearly establish what its proposed measurement adds beyond these ideas.

The empirical evidence supports a narrower conclusion than consistently faster convergence across benchmarks. SPMARL and SPRL are nearly indistinguishable on XOR in Figure 5, and their final performance is generally comparable. Only one target configuration per benchmark is evaluated. There are no sensitivity studies for the important performance threshold or diagnostic ablations addressing critic fitting and return stochasticity, so the robustness and explanation of the observed speedups remain uncertain.

Reproduction from the manuscript requires substantial unspecified choices, including teacher hyperparameters, context initialization and bounds, loss aggregation across agents, and handling the changing action space in XOR. The treatment of discretized or clipped contexts in importance weighting is also unclear. These details can materially affect curriculum behavior. A smaller presentation error is the reference to an eight-agent target in the SMACv2 discussion despite the stated five-versus-five task.
